description:
I'm a software engineering student building Selenic independently. I mainly work with C++, Python and JavaScript, and I'm interested in algorithms, applied mathematics, scientific computing and thoughtful interface design.

My project aims to help users compare lunar south-pole landing sites and dates by visualizing the Sun's position and Earth's visibility. My focus is on clear visualizations, well-structured software, validated calculations and transparent scientific data sources.
summary:
SELENIC is a lunar mission-planning tool designed to help teams evaluate potential landing and operating sites near the Moon’s south pole, where low-angle sunlight and rugged terrain can create long shadows, obstruct solar power, and limit visibility of Earth. The application allows users to compare candidate locations, examine solar and Earth visibility, analyze terrain horizons using compatible elevation data, and explore how changing illumination conditions may affect mission energy availability.

Using NASA/JPL Horizons ephemeris data and user-provided, compatible lunar elevation models, SELENIC combines visibility analysis with a time-stepped power-system simulation. Its goal is to make difficult environmental constraints easier to understand before a mission reaches the lunar surface. By helping planners identify promising operating windows and anticipate potential energy shortfalls, SELENIC supports safer, more informed, and more resilient lunar exploration.

details:
I independently designed and developed SELENIC, a lunar mission-planning application focused on the challenges of operating near the Moon’s south pole.

The lunar south pole is an especially challenging environment because sunlight arrives at very low angles. Nearby ridges can block sunlight, create long shadows, and affect visibility of Earth. These conditions can influence solar energy availability and mission operations.

SELENIC addresses this challenge through several interactive features:

  • Site Comparison: Allows users to compare between two and five candidate lunar locations.
  • Horizon Flip: Demonstrates how terrain can change whether the Sun is visible from a particular location.
  • Visibility Heatmap: Displays changing daily sunlight and visibility conditions over a selected analysis period.
  • Site Ranking: Helps compare locations using configurable considerations such as solar visibility, Earth visibility, and darkness resilience.
  • Mission Simulation: Estimates solar power generation, terrain shading, panel temperature effects, electrical losses, battery state of charge, and unmet energy demand.

The application uses NASA/JPL Horizons ephemeris data to obtain Sun and Earth position information. It also supports compatible, user-provided georeferenced lunar Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) for terrain analysis. The JAXA Kaguya/SELENE SLDEM2013 dataset is a potential terrain-data source, but it must be prepared in a compatible GeoTIFF format before it can be uploaded. It is not preloaded in the application.

I developed the frontend using React, TypeScript, and Vite, with Python and FastAPI powering the backend. Other technologies include SQLite for caching and geospatial processing tools for terrain analysis.

The main creative idea behind SELENIC is that, near the lunar poles, the horizon can determine whether a mission receives sunlight and maintains sufficient energy. Instead of treating a landing location as simply a point on a map, SELENIC helps users understand the relationship between terrain, illumination, visibility, and power availability.

The intended impact is to support better-informed lunar site selection, improve mission preparation, and help planners anticipate difficult operating conditions before deployment.

SELENIC is a planning and educational prototype. Its simulation requires further validation against trusted lunar illumination datasets and engineering reference cases before operational use.
